note: Isomers: same formula, different structures. Stereoisomers: same formula and bonds, different 3-D arrangement. Enantiomers: nonsuperimposable mirror images. Racemic mixture: equal amounts of the two enantiomers.
Only CHFClI has four different atoms on carbon (H, F, Cl, I). CHCl2I repeats Cl, CH2FI repeats H, and CF2ClBr repeats F (RDKit finds a stereocenter only in CHFClI).
Enantiomers have the same formula, bonds, and polarity and differ only in handedness. A binding site built from chiral molecules is itself chiral, so only one mirror-image shape fits it.

Glyceraldehyde C2 (H, OH, CH2OH, CHO) and 1-phenylethanol C1 (H, OH, CH3, C6H5) each carry four different groups. Glycerol (two CH2OH), 2-propanol (two CH3), and CH2BrCl (two H) have none (RDKit agrees).

(a) (−) means levorotatory: the measured rotation is counterclockwise; the R/S label comes from the structure and doesn't predict the sign. (b) In a 50:50 (racemic) mixture, equal and opposite rotations cancel, so there is no net rotation.

In carvone (2-methyl-5-isopropenylcyclohex-2-en-1-one), the stereocenter C5 sits between C4H2, which leads to the C3=C2 double bond, and C6H2, which leads to the C1=O carbonyl. The two ring branches differ beyond their first atom.

C1 (C6H5, OH, H, CH(CH3)NHCH3) and C2 (CH3, H, NHCH3, CH(OH)C6H5) each carry four different groups (RDKit: 2). The NH nitrogen is not counted because amines invert rapidly; a student who counted it would answer 3.

(a) With the C=O replaced by CH2, one ring path from the stereocenter is CH2 then the C=C, and the other is CH2–CH2 then the C=C, so the branches still differ (RDKit finds 1 stereocenter in limonene). (b) A racemic sample's equal and opposite rotations cancel, so there is no net rotation.
An sp3 carbon bonded to four different groups (a stereocenter) is the usual source of chirality. Rings, polar bonds, and C=C bonds do not make a molecule chiral by themselves.
A planar molecule's own plane is a mirror plane, so its mirror image is superimposable. Styrene also has no sp3 carbon to be a stereocenter (RDKit: 0).

NF has 5 + 7 = 12 valence electrons: σ2s² σ*2s² σ2p² π2p⁴ π*2p², so BO = (8 − 4)/2 = 2. By Hund's rule the two π* electrons go into separate orbitals: 2 unpaired, paramagnetic (isoelectronic with O2).
Liquid O2 held between magnet poles is paramagnetic, which requires unpaired electrons (the two π*2p electrons in MO theory).
(a) HeH+ has 2 + 1 − 1 = 2 electrons: σ1s², BO 1. (b) H2²⁻ has 4: σ1s² σ*1s², BO 0. (c) The excited H2 is σ1s¹ σ*1s¹: BO (1 − 1)/2 = 0.
The drawing shows a double bond and two lone pairs on each O, so every electron is paired: 0 unpaired. This is why the Lewis structure cannot explain O2's paramagnetism.

Valence electrons: Li2²⁻ 4 (σ2s² σ*2s², BO 0); Be2²⁺ 2 (σ2s², BO 1); F2²⁺ 12 (BO 2); Ne2²⁺ 14 (BO 1); BN⁻ 3 + 5 + 1 = 9 (BO 2.5). The π/σ ordering doesn't change any of these bond orders, and two rows share bo1.
BF (10 e, ends at π2p⁴) is diamagnetic; CO⁻ (11 e, π*2p¹) is paramagnetic; He2²⁺ (σ1s²) is diamagnetic; OF (13 e, π*2p³) is paramagnetic. Each result is the same under either 2p ordering.
NF (12 e, BO 2) → NF⁺ (11 e) removes an antibonding π* electron, so BO rises to 2.5. The other changes lower BO: Ne2²⁺ 1 → Ne2 0, Be2²⁺ 1 → Be2 0, BF 3 → BF⁻ 2.5.
CF has 11 e: σ2s² σ*2s² σ2p² π2p⁴ π*2p¹, BO (8 − 3)/2 = 2.5, with one unpaired electron, so paramagnetic. CF⁺ has 10 e with π* empty: BO 3.
OF⁺ (12 e) has BO 2, OF (13 e) BO 1.5, and OF⁻ (14 e) BO 1. A lower bond order means a longer bond: OF⁻ > OF > OF⁺.

Be2²⁻ has 6 valence electrons, like B2. With π2p below σ2p the last two go one into each π orbital (paramagnetic); with σ2p lower they pair in σ2p (diamagnetic). He2²⁺ uses only 1s MOs, and CO⁻ (11 e) and Ne2²⁺ (14 e) fill the σ2p/π2p set completely under either order.

The 4 π electrons fill π² n², with π* empty: each N–O link has σ order 1, plus one π bond shared over two links (+0.5), for 1.5. The n MO has a node at N and sits on the two O atoms, so each O averages 2 + ½ = 2.5 lone pairs, matching the average of the resonance structures (2 and 3).
CN⁻ has 4 + 5 + 1 = 10 valence electrons: σ2s² σ*2s² σ2p² π2p⁴, BO (8 − 2)/2 = 3, all paired, so diamagnetic. N2 also has 10 valence electrons and BO 3 (C2 has 8, O2 12, NO 11).
Magnetism depends on unpaired electrons, which only MO theory predicts correctly for O2. Shape is a VSEPR question, bond count a Lewis question, and orbital overlap in CH4 a hybridization question.

Filling from the bottom up puts electrons in each bonding MO before its antibonding partner, so bonding electrons ≥ antibonding electrons and BO ≥ 0. A negative value means a filling or counting error.
NCl3 has 3 bonding pairs + 1 lone pair on N, so SN 4 with tetrahedral electron pairs and a trigonal pyramidal molecular geometry (Day 10 p.26 table).
SiF4 (tetrahedral), BeCl2 (linear), and SO3 (trigonal planar) have symmetric bond dipoles that cancel. CH2O is trigonal planar but its C=O and C–H bonds differ, so the dipoles don't cancel.
The central O in O3 has 2 bonded atoms + 1 lone pair, so SN 3 and sp² hybridization (Table 5.3).
C4H4 has 4 C–H + 3 C–C connections = 7 σ bonds. C≡C has 2 π bonds and C=C has 1, so 3 π (RDKit count agrees).

The real molecule is a single resonance hybrid with two equivalent bonds of order 1.5 (about 128 pm), between O–O 148 pm and O=O 121 pm (Table 4.6). It does not flip between the two structures. The 128 pm value isn't in the course data, but every other option is chemically wrong.
NO2 has 5 + 12 = 17 valence electrons, an odd count, so one electron is unpaired (a free radical). SO2 (18), O3 (18), and CO2 (16) have even counts and are fully paired.
S in SF6 has 6 bonding pairs = 12 electrons (an expanded octet, possible in period 3). N in NF3, C in CF4, and O in OF2 each have exactly 8.
CO2 has SN 2 with no lone pairs on C, so it is linear. SO2, H2O, and O3 have lone pairs on the central atom and are bent.
O3's central O has SN 3 (ideal 120°, measured 117°); water's O has SN 4 (ideal 109.5°, measured 104.5°), per the Day 10 p.13–19 angles in the course data.
In S=C=S the two equal C=S dipoles cancel (and C and S both have EN 2.5 in the course table). In O=C=S the C=O dipole (ΔEN 1.0) is not balanced by C=S, so only OCS is polar.
C3 of 3-methylhexane carries H, CH3, ethyl, and propyl: four different groups. 3-Methylpentane (two ethyls), 2-methylbutane (two CH3), and CH3CHCl2 (two Cl) are achiral (RDKit agrees).
B2 (6 e, π2p², BO 1) → B2²⁻ (8 e, π2p⁴, BO 2): the bond gets stronger. F2 (14 e, BO 1) → F2²⁻ (16 e, σ*2p filled, BO 0): the bond breaks.
C2 uses the Li2–N2 order (π2p below σ2p): 8 valence electrons, σ2s² σ*2s² π2p⁴, BO 2, all paired, so diamagnetic. The σ-below-π order would wrongly give π2p² and paramagnetism (option 0, the trap).
Each ethylene carbon has SN 3 (sp²). Each C–H σ bond is a C sp² hybrid overlapping head-on with an H 1s orbital; hydrogen does not hybridize (Day 11 p.20 rules).
ΔEN from the course values: O–H 1.4, N–H 0.9, C–Cl 0.5, C–H 0.4, so O–H is the most polar.
IF5 has 5 bonding pairs + 1 lone pair on I = SN 6, so the electron-pair geometry is octahedral and the molecular geometry is square pyramidal (Day 10 p.26 table).
The CH3 carbon has four single bonds (SN 4, sp³). The COOH carbon has C=O, C–OH, and C–C (SN 3, sp²).
